Content:
Let's recall the graph of [MATH: y=\sin{x}] once again.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/96a76989651f944931463623c95ebe1e]

Content:
The graph has infinitely many zeros, and there are an infinite number of points where the function reaches its maximum and minimum values. Let's see how to write down general expressions for these properties.

Content:
We'll assume that [MATH: n] represents any integer throughout this discussion.

Content:
The Zeros of the Function

Content:
From the graph, we see that the zeros of the function are [MATH: x=0,\pm\pi, \pm 2\pi\dots.]

Content:
We can write down a general expression for the zeros as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x = n\pi.]

Content:
The Maxima of the Function

Content:
The function has a maximum when [MATH: x=\dfrac\pi 2] and the function is periodic with period [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, a general expression for the values of [MATH: x] that maximize sine is

Content:
[MATH: x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi.]

Content:
The Minima of the Function

Content:
The function has a minimum when [MATH: x=-\dfrac\pi 2] and the function is periodic with period [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, a general expression for the values of [MATH: x] that minimize sine is

Content:
[MATH: x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2n\pi.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's plot the graph of [MATH: y=\sin{x}.]

Let's go through each statement.

  • Statement I is false. The zeros occur at [MATH: x=0, \pm \pi, \pm 2\pi,\ldots,] which can be written as [MATH: x=n\pi.]

  • Statement II is true. The function has a minimum at [MATH: x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2},] and the period is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, the minimum values occur at [MATH: -\dfrac{\pi}{2}+2n\pi.]

  • Statement III is true. The function has a maximum at [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},] and the period is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, the maximum values occur at [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2}+2n\pi.]

items.title: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Sine Function

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \sin x = \dfrac{1}2,] then what is [MATH: -2\sin(x+6\pi)-3?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \sin x = \dfrac{1}2,] then what is [MATH: -2\sin(x+6\pi)-3?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of [MATH: y = \sin x] is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, for any integer [MATH: n] we have

[MATH: \sin{x} = \sin{(x+2n\pi)} .]

Substituting [MATH: n=3] into the above gives

[MATH: \sin x|= \sin (x + 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ π); = \sin (x + 6π).]

Therefore, if [MATH: \sin{x} = \dfrac{1}{2},] then [MATH: \sin{(x+6\pi)} = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Finally, then:

[MATH: − 2\sin (x + 6π) − 3|= − 2((1)/(2)) − 3; = − 1 − 3; = − 4.]

Content:
Recall that a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if it satisfies the property

Content:
[MATH: f(-x) = -f(x).]

Content:
As it turns out, sine is an odd function! So, for any value of [MATH: x,] we have
[MATH: \sin(-x) = -\sin(x).]

Content:
Odd functions always have rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This is indeed true of the sine function, as we can see from the diagram below.

Graphic:

Content:
We can use the oddness property of sine in conjunction with its periodicity property to simplify trigonometric expressions. Let's see an example.

items.title: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Sine Function

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \sin{x} = -\dfrac{4}{7},] then what is the value of [MATH: \sin(-x + 16 \pi)?]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \sin{x} = -\dfrac{4}{7},] then what is the value of [MATH: \sin(-x + 16 \pi)?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y = \sin{x}.]

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of [MATH: \sin{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]

  • Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \sin{x}] is an odd function, and we have [MATH: \sin(-x) = -\sin{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \sin{x},] we have [MATH: \sin (− x + 16π)|= \sin (− x + 2π ⋅ 8); = \sin (− x).]

  • Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \sin{x},] we have [MATH: \sin (− x)|= − \sin x; = − (− (4)/(7)); = (4)/(7).]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin(-x + 16\pi) = \dfrac{4}{7}.]

The periodicity of [MATH: y=\sin x] means that [MATH: \sin\left( x+2n\pi\right) = \sin\left( x\right)] for any number [MATH: x] and [MATH: n] is any integer.

Item 6 — Example: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Sine Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \sin x = \dfrac{1}2,] then what is [MATH: -2\sin(x+6\pi)-3?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The period of [MATH: y = \sin x] is [MATH: 2\pi.] Therefore, for any integer [MATH: n] we have

[MATH: \sin{x} = \sin{(x+2n\pi)} .]

Substituting [MATH: n=3] into the above gives

[MATH: \sin x|= \sin (x + 2 ⋅ 3 ⋅ π); = \sin (x + 6π).]

Therefore, if [MATH: \sin{x} = \dfrac{1}{2},] then [MATH: \sin{(x+6\pi)} = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Finally, then:

[MATH: − 2\sin (x + 6π) − 3|= − 2((1)/(2)) − 3; = − 1 − 3; = − 4.]

Content:
Recall that a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if it satisfies the property

Content:
As it turns out, sine is an odd function! So, for any value of [MATH: x,] we have
[MATH: \sin(-x) = -\sin(x).]

Item 10 — Example: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Sine Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \sin{x} = -\dfrac{4}{7},] then what is the value of [MATH: \sin(-x + 16 \pi)?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y = \sin{x}.]

[IMG: /graphics/354416a40760fc1b81921d9a6c096adf]

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of [MATH: \sin{x}] is [MATH: 2\pi.]
- Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \sin{x}] is an odd function, and we have
[MATH: \sin(-x) = -\sin{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \sin{x},] we have
[MATH: \sin (− x + 16π)|= \sin (− x + 2π ⋅ 8); = \sin (− x).]
- Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \sin{x},] we have
[MATH: \sin (− x)|= − \sin x; = − (− (4)/(7)); = (4)/(7).]

Therefore, [MATH: \sin(-x + 16\pi) = \dfrac{4}{7}.]
